title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
body_text: A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth | GPU Partner Skip to content GPU partner Inventory ▾ Systems Memory Storage GPU Cloud Compute View all inventory → Resources ▾ Blog Announcements VRAM calculator Reference Workloads Contact About Build a system Reach a human Build a system Reach a human Home / Blog A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. By Jerry James · Nov 22, 2026 With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware. Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too. Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times). The short version Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it. What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home? Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list: A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup. Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth . An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section. That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required. Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run? It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations. On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in. What Is Quantization? Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster. The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2. If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable. Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM? For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits. Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator . At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare. If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs . If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start. Size VRAM Models to try Version (quant) Context size Cards at this size Small 8-12 GB Qwen3.5-9B , Gemma 4 12B UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M 8K-16K RTX 5060 8GB , RTX 3060 12GB , RTX 5070 12GB Medium 16 GB Qwen3-14B , gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE) Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M 16K-32K RTX 5060 Ti 16GB , RTX 5070 Ti , RTX 5080 , RTX PRO 2000 Large 24 GB Gemma 4 31B , Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S 16K-32K RTX 3090 , RTX 4090 , RX 7900 XTX , RTX PRO 4000 Extra Large 32 GB+ Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K 64K-128K+ RTX 5090 32GB , RTX PRO 4500 32GB , RTX PRO 5000 48GB , RTX PRO 6000 96GB Small VRAM 8-12 GB Models to try Qwen3.5-9B , Gemma 4 12B Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M Context size 8K-16K Cards at this size RTX 5060 8GB , RTX 3060 12GB , RTX 5070 12GB Medium VRAM 16 GB Models to try Qwen3-14B , gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE) Version (quant) Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M Context size 16K-32K Cards at this size RTX 5060 Ti 16GB , RTX 5070 Ti , RTX 5080 , RTX PRO 2000 Large VRAM 24 GB Models to try Gemma 4 31B , Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S Context size 16K-32K Cards at this size RTX 3090 , RTX 4090 , RX 7900 XTX , RTX PRO 4000 Extra Large VRAM 32 GB+ Models to try Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K Context size 64K-128K+ Cards at this size RTX 5090 32GB , RTX PRO 4500 32GB , RTX PRO 5000 48GB , RTX PRO 6000 96GB Models marked MoE ( mixture of experts ) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way. Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate. Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090? Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no. Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context. Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2. Inkling 2 Mini Memory needed Fits entirely on 2-bit 10-11 GB 12 GB card 3-bit 13-15 GB 16 GB card 4-bit (recommended) 17-18 GB 24 GB card 8-bit (lossless) 24 GB 32 GB card 2-bit Memory needed 10-11 GB Fits entirely on 12 GB card 3-bit Memory needed 13-15 GB Fits entirely on 16 GB card 4-bit (recommended) Memory needed 17-18 GB Fits entirely on 24 GB card 8-bit (lossless) Memory needed 24 GB Fits entirely on 32 GB card Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower. Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station , not a graphics card. Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac? Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory . Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon. The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark . How Do You Set Up a Local AI with Unsloth Desktop? It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along. Step 1: Install Unsloth Desktop First, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup. I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription. The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor. Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one. Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded. Step 2: Download a Quantized Model On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B. The model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list. You should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU. Every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting. Step 3: Set the Context Size Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need. I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU . At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth. Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup. How Do You Share a Local AI Across Your Home Network? Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network. Once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC. Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab. Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part. Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set. Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it. Can You Access Your Local AI Across the Internet? Soon™ Not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network. If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away. In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship. As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help. PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go! An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the service and installed malware on some of those devices. We blocked the identified attack path on November 20 and released security firmware that disables the known malware and removes the related files and traces identified during our investigation. We have submitted CVE reports for the vulnerabilities identified during our investigation into the attack and malware; CVE identifiers are pending. See technical details. Who is affected Receiving this notice, seeing an update prompt, or finding your model in the download tables does not mean your device was accessed. This incident involved devices connected to GoodCloud; a connection alone does not establish that an attack occurred. Your situation What it means and what to do Your device never connected to GoodCloud It was not likely exposed through this incident's attack path. Update the firmware as routine security maintenance. This incident alone is not a reason to reset the device or replace passwords and keys. Your device connected to GoodCloud, but you have no evidence of unauthorized access It may have been exposed, but compromise is not confirmed. Install the security firmware and follow the precautionary password and key guidance below. GL.iNet identified your device as affected, or you have evidence or a reasonable suspicion of unauthorized access Follow the recovery guidance below. If access appears to be ongoing, contain it first. For an affected KVM, also check the connected computer as a precaution. Some KVM devices have cloud service enabled before account linking. Not having a cloud account, or not linking a device, is not by itself proof that it never connected. See the KVM cloud-service documentation . If you are unsure about the device's connection history or a suspicious change, contact Support for help assessing it. What you should do now For all users: install the security firmware Install the latest stable security firmware for your exact model , using the official links below. You can update through the device's administration page; you do not need to run terminal commands or a security check first. Follow the router upgrade guide or KVM upgrade guide . An update is a preventive step for users without evidence of compromise. An update prompt alone does not require a reset or password changes. If you want an optional check or need to preserve evidence, do that before restarting, resetting, or updating, since those actions can remove signs of earlier activity. If unauthorized access is known or suspected: contain and recover If access appears to be ongoing, disconnect the device from the internet if you can do so safely and contact Support from another device. If disconnecting would cut off your only remote access, contact Support to plan recovery. For the strongest standard recovery assurance, download the official security firmware, install it without keeping settings, and manually configure the device again. Use new passwords and keys, and do not restore a backup from a potentially compromised device. On routers, turn Keep Settings off; on KVMs that offer it, clear Save current configuration . The upgrade guides above explain these options. If your model's options differ, ask Support for the appropriate procedure. A factory reset alone does not install the security fixes. Keeping settings remains an option you may choose , including to preserve remote access. The update still provides targeted cleanup for the known November 20 malware and can substantially reduce the risk from that malware. However, it may retain other unauthorized changes, so it provides less recovery assurance than reinstalling without settings. Contact Support if you need help choosing an approach or suspicious activity continues. For an affected KVM, also check the attached computer for unfamiliar accounts, software, browser extensions, startup items, or unexpected settings changes, and run a full scan with current security software. This is a precaution; it does not mean the attached computer was also accessed. See the KVM guidance in the incident announcement . If your device connected to GoodCloud: replace potentially exposed passwords and keys After updating or recovering the device, change passwords and replace access keys stored on or accessible from the GL.iNet device as a precaution, even if a check finds nothing. Examples include its administrator password and, if used, VPN and SSH keys. This advice does not mean every connected device was accessed or every password was copied. An update cannot revoke a key or password that was already copied. For other computers and devices, replace credentials if they were also stored on the GL.iNet device, reused there, or there is evidence or a reasonable suspicion that the other device was accessed. Simply connecting a computer by Ethernet or Wi-Fi does not, by itself, establish that its passwords were exposed. If you are unsure which credentials need changing, ask Support. The technical discussion of credential exposure explains why these precautions matter after unauthorized administrator access. Download and install the security update The security firmware disables the known malware from this incident and removes its related files and the traces identified during our investigation , including when settings are retained. It provides targeted cleanup; it is not a general malware scan or a complete integrity check. Additional vulnerability fixes and their cloud or firmware coverage are explained in Technical details and investigation findings . The cloud-side fix blocked the identified attack path, while firmware cleanup addresses the known malware already on a device. Neither can undo past access or revoke copied credentials. Follow the recovery guidance above if access is known or suspected. These tables list models with published security firmware, not confirmed compromised models. Install the latest stable release for your exact model; the versions below are the minimum security versions listed in this notice. If you installed a security beta, move to the latest stable release. Router security firmware downloads Model Minimum security version GL-MG1300 , GL-MT3000 , GL-MT6000 4.11.1 GL-E5800 4.10.3 GL-BE3600 , GL-BE9300 4.10.2 GL-BE14000 4.9.3 GL-BE6500 , GL-MT3600BE , GL-MT5000 4.9.1 GL-BE10000 4.8.7 GL-AX1800 , GL-AXT1800 , GL-SFT1200 , GL-X3000 , GL-XE3000 4.8.4 GL-MT2500 / GL-MT2500A , GL-X2000 4.7.14 GL-AXT1800: Install the security build from the official link above. If your device already shows 4.8.4 and you are unsure which build is installed, contact Support . KVM security firmware downloads Model Minimum security version RM1 , RM1V2 , RM10 , RM10RC , RM1PE , RM4PE 1.10.3 RMQ1 1.8.7 If your model is not listed, check the GL.iNet Download Center or ask Support which update applies. Do not install another model's firmware. The table is an update list, not a determination of which individual devices were affected. Optional device checks before updating Updating is the primary action. A check is optional and is not a prerequisite for installing the security firmware. If you want to check first, do so before restarting, resetting, or updating. Neither method below can rule out previous access or certify that a device is free of compromise. First choice for broader coverage: community security check The independently maintained community security check examines files, startup entries, running processes, and network connections for a broader set of known indicators. It can also flag indicators of the separate router persistence finding described below. This is an independent third-party project. Review its instructions and source code , and use check-only mode. Administrator access is required. Skip evidence collection, cleanup, and report submission if you only want to check. An unfamiliar change flagged for review is not automatically proof of infection. You may ask Support for help instead of running a script. Optional KVM check — limited coverage See the KVM quick-check instructions on the GL.iNet forum . A negative result does not rule out compromise; follow this bulletin's firmware and recovery guidance. Technical details and investigation findings How the incident happened GoodCloud's MQTT device-messaging service, deployed using EMQX, had a configuration error in message authorization. A client could send management messages to other users' connected devices without the required permission. This is a finding about GL.iNet's GoodCloud deployment , not a claim that every EMQX installation is vulnerable. The GoodCloud report describes the service-side authorization problem. A separate AstroWarp/SD-WAN input-handling flaw could cause management input to be executed as commands with root (administrator) privileges on affected routers, even when AstroWarp was turned off. A community report documents unauthorized remote command access on a GoodCloud-connected router. The RTTY finding below concerns remote-terminal connection security. These are distinct issues; the router command-injection flaw should not be assumed to explain every KVM compromise. Vulnerability reports and remediation coverage The links below point to GL.iNet's published vulnerability reports. Official CVE identifiers remain subject to assignment/publication confirmation ; report titles and internal tracking references are not CVE numbers. Vulnerability report Security impact Remediation and firmware coverage GoodCloud message authorization — GitHub report Unauthorized messages could change device configuration or invoke device management APIs. Further impact depends on what the device accepts and processes. The report identifies GoodCloud v3.19.13 as affected and v3.19.14 as fixed. The identified cloud attack path was blocked on November 20. This is a service-side fix; device firmware separately provides incident malware cleanup. AstroWarp/SD-WAN command injection — GitHub report Insufficient input validation could allow root command execution on the listed routers, including with AstroWarp disabled. The report lists model-specific expected fix versions. The download tables above identify published incident security releases; check the exact model and build. The report's planned-version wording alone does not verify every shipped build. This router finding is not a KVM vulnerability claim. RTTY configuration and TLS certificate verification — GitHub report If relevant startup arguments can be modified, intended server-certificate verification can be bypassed, allowing connection to an attacker-controlled terminal server and root access. The report identifies 1.10.3 as fixed for RM1, RM10, RM10RC, RM1PE, RM1V2, and RM4PE, and 1.8.7 for RMQ1. Its router entries use expected fix wording; those entries do not by themselves confirm publication or verification of every planned router fix. Fixing a vulnerability and cleaning up a compromised device are different tasks. The versions above describe the linked reports' remediation status; they are not a finding that every listed device was attacked. Retained settings, copied credentials, and changes outside the targeted cleanup can still require recovery action. Additional findings and recovery limits Separate router persistence reports. Community users reported a modified startup script and suspicious processes; GL.iNet acknowledged these reports in the forum . Some reported file dates predate November 20. The original reports do not establish the initial entry path or a connection to this incident. A process name alone is not proof of infection. Do not assume incident malware cleanup resolves every separate persistence finding. Why keeping settings can leave other changes. Community KVM testing reported that an added startup script and SSH key survived a configuration-preserving upgrade on a test RM1. This illustrates a recovery limit; it does not establish that every affected KVM had those modifications. For known or suspected compromise, reinstall without keeping configuration using the model's supported upgrade options. Firmware and boot integrity. Community recovery analysis explains that a normal reset or firmware reinstall may not rewrite every flash region. This is a recovery limitation, not evidence that boot components were changed in this attack. Contact Support if there are reasons to suspect deeper changes or activity persists after recovery. Other devices and credentials. We have not confirmed access to other devices through a compromised GL.iNet device. However, root access can expose credentials held on that device, as explained in the remote-access case report . Not confirming access to another device does not eliminate that credential risk. Investigation and further updates Security firmware has already been released for the models listed above. Its availability does not mean every device of those models was compromised, and additional findings do not establish that all listed devices share the same vulnerabilities. We are continuing to determine the number of affected devices, the timeline of unauthorized activity, and whether computers connected to affected KVMs were accessed. As individual findings are verified, we will update this notice and publish model-specific advisories identifying the relevant versions, confirmed fixes, and any further actions. Any additional firmware work will be described separately from the security releases already available. Our commitment to customers We’re sorry for the concern and disruption this incident caused. Updating and recovering devices takes time, especially when they are managed remotely. Our Support team is ready to help you assess your device, choose a recovery approach, and interpret check results. Teams across GL.iNet are continuing the investigation and adding safeguards to our cloud services and device firmware. We will share confirmed findings and further guidance as they become available. Frequently asked questions 1. Was my device affected by this incident? Devices that never connected to GoodCloud were not exposed through this incident's attack path. Devices that connected could have been exposed, but connection alone does not establish compromise. AstroWarp being turned off does not rule out GoodCloud exposure. Some KVMs can connect before account linking. If your connection history is unclear, contact Support. Keep firmware up to date as routine security maintenance. 2. Does a check that finds nothing mean my device was unaffected? No. A check covers only the indicators it looks for, and restarting or updating can remove signs. Install the security firmware regardless of the result. For optional checks, use the community check for routers or broader KVM coverage. The short KVM check has limited coverage. 3. Who needs to change passwords and keys or check other devices? For devices that connected to GoodCloud, and for any device you know or suspect was compromised, replace credentials stored on or accessible from the device after updating or recovery. This is a precaution even without a positive check. A device that never connected and has no other reason to suspect compromise does not need incident-related credential replacement. Check the computer attached to an affected KVM; for other devices, use the exposure and access criteria in What you should do now . 4. Can the same GoodCloud attack path still be used? We blocked the identified attack path on November 20. That service-side fix does not remove malware already installed on a device. Install the security firmware and follow the recovery guidance appropriate to your situation. The vulnerability reports above describe the scope of each fix. 5. Will I receive an email if my device was affected? We will email customers whose devices we identify as affected using the address associated with their GL.iNet cloud account, including when a device has since been rebooted or updated. Not receiving an email is not proof that a device was unaffected. Do not wait for a notification before installing the security firmware or seeking help if you suspect compromise. 6. Do I need to factory reset or reinstall firmware? An update prompt alone is not a reason to reset. If unauthorized access is known or suspected, the strongest standard recovery option is to reinstall official security firmware without preserving settings, then manually configure the device again. Turn off Keep Settings on a router or Save current configuration on a supported KVM upgrade. Keeping settings remains your choice, with the cleanup limits explained above. A reset alone does not install the fixes. See the linked upgrade guides or ask Support about your model. Contact For device checks, firmware updates, and recovery, email support@gl-inet.com . To report a security issue, email security@gl-inet.com . Update history November 20, 2026 (UTC): Initial notice issued. November 22, 2026 (UTC): Added the community security check and further information. November 23, 2026 (UTC): Updated with pending CVE reports(identifies pending assessment) and additional findings. title: Perplexity and Intelligence
body_text: Perplexity and Intelligence | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI November 22, 2026 Research Safety Perplexity and Intelligence By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI Share From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts. A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation. The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5. The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4 , GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric. As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative. A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining. We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5 . While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining. Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation ⁠ (opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits , based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development. Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges: Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models. Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities. Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities. Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence. At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry. Compute Scaling Ethics & Safety 2026 Author Jakub Pachocki Footnotes 1 It’s important to note that “compressor” in this sense is something that is capable of performing compression by predicting unseen data, not a compressed artifact like a GZIP file - that is, the best compressor trained on a given corpus does not necessarily “remember” the contents of the corpus. 2 In practice, we generally track the log of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss . 3 The primary held-out datasets we’ve been using since GPT-3.5 are sourced from our internal codebase, and those are the numbers reported here (for a fixed snapshot). 4 Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI. 5 On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI ⁠ . Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA Pancreas cancer Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’ Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing Helena Horton Fri 20 Nov 2026 04.36 EST Last modified on Sat 21 Nov 2026 00.07 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission. ‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcast Read more Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally. Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans. A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread. He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said. FDA gives expedited approval to new groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug Read more “The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.” Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth. There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations. Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers. “These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.” Explore more on these topics Pancreas cancer Cancer research Medical research Drugs Health news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day 5 Nov 2026 Woman told she had cancer by NHS worker who inappropriately accessed her records 21 Oct 2026 New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests 19 Oct 2026 Pope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next? 16 Oct 2026 Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgery 13 Oct 2026 double quotation mark The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted 8 Oct 2026 ‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle 8 Oct 2026 Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds 6 Oct 2026 Cancer jab can eradicate entire tumours in patients, trial shows 30 May 2026 Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies.
