results/COMPLETENESS.md Write-ups of the compiler on SmolLM2-360M and Qwen3.5-4B, and of the reproduction check site/ The website: the front page, and each paper in its own folder ( compiler/ , 2/ , grafting/ ). Run python3 -m http.server 8000 inside it, then visit http://localhost:8000 tests/ Tests of the grammar and the codes The tests need SmolLM2-360M and WikiText-2 Each test file runs on its own from the repository root, and all seven finish in under a minute. python tests/test_frame.py python tests/test_grammar.py python tests/test_codes.py python tests/test_elements.py python tests/test_nested.py python tests/test_rowgroup_alloc.py python tests/test_reallocation.py runtime_mlx/test_core.py checks the runtime against the quantizer's math. Run python runtime_mlx/make_ref.py first, which writes 1.6 GB of reference files. runtime_mlx/test_fast_q35.py and runtime_mlx/test_block_q35.py check the Qwen3.5 kernels against NumPy products of independently unpacked codes, with no model. When LAMQ_Q35_PACKED names a packed file, the second also checks a block of tokens against decoding them one at a time. When LAMQ_Q38_PACKED names the packed Qwen3.8-27B file, it runs the same checks on a model whose output head is stored apart from its embedding. runtime_mlx/test_inkling.py checks the Inkling-2-Mini runtime on a miniature packed model it builds, including chunked prefill and PromptCache reuse against a fresh prefill. runtime_mlx/test_server.py checks lamq serve 's output parsing, message conversion and HTTP layer, with no model. python -m pytest runtime_cuda/ exercises the CUDA runtimes. GPU kernel checks use synthetic inputs. Checkpoint comparisons also require the packed weights and their reference outputs. What this repository leaves out Model weights. Everything downloads from Hugging Face. The Qwen3.5-4B jobs expect that model in models/Qwen3.5-4B on the volume. Benchmark copies. eval_tasks.py downloads its benchmarks. On an offline machine it reads exported copies from data/bench/ , which are not here. The Modal images run offline, so cache the benchmarks on the volume first. The script that assembled site/data.json . It was a set of one-off steps. The source numbers are all in results/ . LookAtMyQuant 2's dense weights and result files. The 1.2 GB file is a release in the packed format. The dense weights the benchmarks ran on are not published, and neither are the per-problem results behind site2/data.json or the script that writes the page's numbers from them. The drafter at 16 bits. The drafter as trained is 1.8 GB and is not published. The 4-bit one is a release file, and modal_drafter.py trains it. We took eight ideas from Cary Palmer's Kintsugi Cary Palmer's Kintsugi method paper measured our 8.9 GB Inkling-2-Mini build against Kintsugi for Inkling 2 Mini and split the KL by kind of text. The two builds tied on overall KL, and ours was 25% lower on prose. It was higher on code (+29%), tool calls (+35%), agentic text (+83%) and reasoning (+74%). Our calibration text had not been rendered in Inkling's chat template, and our expert Hessians saw only the tokens routed to each expert. We took these ideas from the two Kintsugi repositories to close that gap: Idea from Kintsugi Where it is here Each expert's Hessian comes from every calibration token, not only the tokens routed to it --dense-expert-h in compiler.py measure and quantize.py Calibration text is rendered in the model's own chat template, and KL is scored separately for prose, code, tools, agentic text, reasoning and multilingual text --data templated and --per-class in compiler.py measure A plan is judged by its worst kind of text as well as by its mean KL --max-class-ratio and --class-weights in compiler.py allocate Recall of a fact or a code copy deep in a long prompt is scored as a teacher-forced margin, against the same item placed close by The recall check we run on new Inkling-2-Mini builds Sliding-window attention caches stay small FP16 rings, the global attention caches are stored at q8_0 or q4_0 , and cache cells past a VRAM limit move to pinned host memory LAMQ_CUDA_GLOBAL_KV and LAMQ_CUDA_KV_VRAM_CELLS in the CUDA runtime A long chat is saved to disk, so it continues after a restart without reading the prompt again --prompt-cache-dir and --prompt-cache-gb in lamq serve When an agent repeats nearly the same tool call, the server adds one short note to the request On by default in lamq serve ; --no-repeat-guard turns it off Claude Code and Codex connect directly through Anthropic's /v1/messages and OpenAI's /v1/responses , with developer messages read as system lamq serve Two runtime speedups follow Actual's aci-cpp Justin Bennington's post In Search of Perfection: aci-cpp vs. llama.cpp describes aci-cpp, Actual's fork of llama.cpp. We built two of its ideas from that description: Idea from aci-cpp Where it is here Gated DeltaNet prefill runs as fused, chunked kernels runtime_mlx/fast_q35.py , which makes Qwen3.8-27B prefill 16% to 37% faster on an M5 Max at 256 to 2,048 prompt tokens Decoding over a very long attention span gets a faster way to read the cache Inkling decoding in runtime_mlx/inkling/fast_kernels.py , which splits long spans 32 or 64 ways Thank you to everyone who has contributed Contributor Contribution Patrick Dugan The native CUDA engine for the packed Inkling-2-Mini files, with DSpark verification and a chat server ( runtime_cuda/inkling_cuda/ ) Ian B The Triton CUDA runtime for packed Inkling-2-Mini models ( runtime_cuda/inkling/ ) Mark Pesce lamq serve with prompt caching, and chunked Inkling prefill so long prompts fit in memory Noah Lindner Trellis tables staged in threadgroup memory for Qwen and Inkling decoding, after reporting slow decoding on M1 Pro Dmitry (Dee) Kargaev Apple M4 Metal tuning, the fp8 and q4 global KV cache, and the fix for the DSpark threadgroup crash on M1 to M3 Dung Duc Huynh The report of the Metal threadgroup crash on M1 Max Max Ng Inkling kernels that launch within the M1's threadgroup limits Amlandeep Bhadra The browser chat page for lamq serve ( --ui ) About A quantization compiler that delivers 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size lookatmyquant.com Resources Readme MIT license Activity Stars 701 stars Watchers 3 watching Forks 38 forks Report repository Releases Packages Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. Huang’s Return Is the Biggest National Security Scandal in U.S. History Trump has put his pocketbook first and U.S. interests last. Palmer-James-foreign-policy-columnist20 James Palmer By James Palmer , a deputy editor at Foreign Policy . Jensen Huang, wearing a black leather jacket, dark pants, and glasses, stands on a bright stage flanked by tall rows of dark server racks during a keynote presentation. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers the keynote address during the Nvidia GTC 2025 in San Jose, California, on March 18, 2025. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Get audio access with any FP subscription. LOGIN November 23, 2026, 2:06 PM Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov. 12 after his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was exposed and it became apparent that Nvidia was complicit in China’s evasion of U.S. export controls. Now, under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang, saying that senior government officials promised that he posed “no national security risk.” This may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace on Nov. 12 after his affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was exposed and it became apparent that Nvidia was complicit in China’s evasion of U.S. export controls. Now, under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Nvidia’s board has reinstated Jensen Huang, saying that senior government officials promised that he posed “no national security risk.” This may be the biggest national security scandal in U.S. history. That is a high bar. Consider the nearest competitor, the Iran-Contra affair. Officials in U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s administration, with the president’s knowledge , secretly sold weapons to Iran during the Iran-Iraq War, circumventing an arms embargo that Reagan publicly supported. They did so both to secure Iran’s help in freeing U.S. hostages in Lebanon and to raise money for the Contras, a far-right Nicaraguan militant organization whose members committed atrocities against Nicaraguans and Americans alike. Once investigations began, officials orchestrated a cover-up . Reagan’s successor pardoned six individuals connected to the affair. As morally foul as Iran-Contra was, it did not involve personal profiteering by the president and his associates. Nor did it involve the United States helping its principal geopolitical rival. Now, consider what is known about the Jensen Huang affair. China and the United States are locked in an intense race over artificial intelligence. Compute—the raw processing power that depends on advanced chips—is central to that contest. The United States has an unusually powerful position in this market, as most advanced chips are designed by Nvidia and largely manufactured by the Taiwanese firm TSMC. Both Nvidia and the White House were warned that Jensen Huang—a close Trump ally—was having an affair with a Chinese spy, including in a memo to senior officials overseen by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But neither Trump nor Nvidia acted on these warnings. Meanwhile, U.S. tech policy underwent a dramatic reversal. Last December, Nvidia struck a deal with the White House to sell its H200 chips to China in exchange for a 25 percent cut for the U.S. government, with no public details about how the funds will be used or overseen. Huang donated $25 million to the president’s ballroom, and Trump owns large amounts of Nvidia stock. When news of the affair broke shortly after the U.S. midterms, it set off a cascade of revelations and investigations . Alice Huang, along with her husband and her business partner in Singapore, were found in multiple outlets’ reporting to be deeply involved in a network of firms allegedly established to evade U.S. restrictions and funnel advanced chips to China. Lawmakers also released information that revealed Nvidia had shipped more than 800,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 11, including to firms closely linked to the Chinese military. A struggle broke out within Trump’s court, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for failing to prevent China from accessing these chips. On top of that, Jensen Huang reportedly had another affair with a direct report and presided over an allegedly abusive workplace culture at Nvidia. Trump’s response was to pressure Nvidia’s board for Huang’s reinstatement, potentially signaling that his administration would protect the company from punishment for its misdeeds. By Trump’s own admission , the decision followed a lengthy conversation with Chinese President Xi Jinping about the Nvidia leader. On Friday, Trump issued an executive order attempting to forestall congressional investigation into the deal. The immediate beneficiary, apart from Nvidia’s stock price, is Beijing. China can now dismiss U.S. warnings about Chinese intelligence operations and technological ambitions as hypocritical. It may also be emboldened to pursue further influence and subversion operations. Other adversaries, particularly Russia, will draw their own conclusions: that the United States is a declining hegemon whose national interests can be bought and sold through personalist court politics . The scandal is unlikely to disappear quietly. Concerned intelligence and national security officials may continue leaking documents about Nvidia, potentially exposing other instances of corruption. Democrats will take this up as a major issue in the new Congress in January, and some Republicans may even join them. The U.S. media now has a choice. It can treat this as a major national scandal, as it did Hillary Clinton’s emails in 2016 or Harvard President Claudine Gay’s improper academic citations in 2023, with front-page scrutiny for weeks or months. Or it can treat the affair as just another episode of the Trump show, or as a partisan political issue, and move on. Supposed China hawks in the Trump administration, including Rubio and Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, face a similar choice. They can resign in protest, drawing national attention to the scandal and positioning themselves as a different kind of Republican for a future, cleaner administration. Or they can continue serving a president that puts his pocketbook ahead of national security. But they cannot keep telling themselves that they can make a difference from the inside. Rewrite the 5% that's slow. Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/ . Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway. fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible. Install npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything # or: cargo install fast-anything Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain ( rustup ). Use fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py # or: -- node app.ts / bun app.ts / deno run -A app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c / Rscript app.R Or step by step: command what it does scan -- <cmd> profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are port [id] records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + TASK.md verify release-builds the port and replays every recorded call enable / disable swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte) bench times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs report markdown + SVG card for your PR doctor checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents --agent takes claude , codex , or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use. Proof, not vibes That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time. Results Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from examples/ . app before after Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) 4.91s 42ms, 116× TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) 3.11s 155ms, 20× PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) 2.94s 53ms, 55× Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) 3.02s 144ms, 21× Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) 3.13s 228ms, 14× C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 4.03s 312ms, 13× Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 3.50s 1.18s, 3× (11× on the function; the rest is JVM startup) C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) 431ms 127ms, 3.4× C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) 3.02s 1.09s, 2.7× fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×. Why not rewrite it all? Compile time : each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes. Cache : every port shares one .fast/target . Delete it whenever you like ( fast-anything clean ). Risk : your code stays as it is. Rust is opt-in per function, checked against real behavior. Agents Claude Code plugin : /plugin marketplace add EL4CTEO/fast-anything , then /plugin install fast-anything@fast-anything and /fast-anything:fast python app.py MCP server (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…), built into the binary: claude mcp add fast-anything -- fast-anything mcp . 8 tools: fast_scan , fast_port , fast_verify , fast_enable , fast_disable , fast_bench , fast_report , fast_status . Skill : skills/fast-anything teaches any agent the loop. Languages language binding status Python 3.10+ PyO3 ✅ JavaScript / TypeScript (Node 22+, Bun, Deno 2+: bun app.ts , deno run -A app.ts ) napi-rs ✅ Ruby 3.3+ C ABI + JSON, through Ruby's built-in Fiddle ✅ Java 22+ ( java App.java , Maven, Gradle) the same C bridge, through the FFM API ✅ Kotlin/JVM (Gradle, src/main/kotlin , JDK 22+) the Java bridge; top-level functions, object and companion members, extension functions ✅ Go 1.22+ ( go run . ) the same C bridge, through the Windows loader or dlopen (cgo) ✅ PHP 8.1+ ( php app.php ) the same C bridge, through PHP's FFI extension ( extension=ffi ) ✅ C and C++ (gcc, clang or Intel oneAPI icx/icpx: clang -O2 main.c lib.c ) the same C bridge, through LoadLibrary or dlopen ✅ C# / .NET 8+ ( dotnet run -c Release ) the same C bridge, through NativeLibrary; profiled with EventPipe, nothing to install; GUIs and servers: scan --duration 30 ✅ R 4.0+ ( Rscript app.R ) the same C bridge, through base R's .C() ; profiled with Rprof, no packages or R headers needed ✅ It ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, typed arrays…), including ones in your entry script when its main code sits under if __name__ == "__main__": (or if __FILE__ == $0 , or if (import.meta.main) / if (require.main === module) ). In Python that means module-level functions and @staticmethod s (dataclasses, NamedTuples and numeric NumPy arrays count as plain data), in Java, C# and PHP static methods (and PHP functions), in Go plain functions, in C and C++ free functions and static methods. scan says why anything else can't move yet. With Intel oneAPI on Windows, run fast-anything from a shell where setvars.bat ran (it sets up the linker). SYCL kernels run on the device and aren't ported; with -fsycl , only host functions are profiled and ported. Ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C, C++, C# and R need no headers, bindings or extra tools: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly. Any language that can call C can use that bridge. License MIT About Don't rewrite it in Rust. title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
body_text: My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75% :: The Tymscar Blog Tymscar My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75% 2026-11-15 Oscar Molnar 8 min read (1684 words) # networking   # debugging   # apple   # macOS   # usb   # unifi   Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite! My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed. I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency. But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR . I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦 The setup # MacBook Pro M3 Pro 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post What I thought was interesting # Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know. I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again. So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason. The driver and flow control # The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website , so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault. Then I tried flow control . I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast… I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be. But the upload was always fine # Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be! Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames: Sent Lost behind the display Frames/s reaching the Mac behind the display Lost direct on the Mac 1.46 Gbps 0% 123,800 0% 1.75 Gbps 0.05% 148,600 0% 1.94 Gbps 0.1% 165,000 0% 2.03 Gbps 2.7% 168,000 0% 2.12 Gbps 7.2% 168,000 0% 2.20 Gbps 10.5% 168,000 0.001% 2.28 Gbps 13.5% 168,000 0.02% So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped. Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts! When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4. Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job. As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is. Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this. OK, well, what now? # I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask. The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1… So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter . My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did! With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames: Sent Frames/s reaching the Mac Dropped by the adapter 1.5 Gbps 124k 0 1.9 Gbps 157k 0 2.1 Gbps 173k 0 2.3 Gbps 187k 0 2.4 Gbps 194k 0 Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself: $ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])" # old adapter (RTL8156B) packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3 # new adapter (RTL8157) packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7 # bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8 I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac. Final thoughts # I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets? See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from! Read other posts [ Ctrl+F Finds Words. I Wanted It to Find Answers. ] > © 2026 Powered by Hugo :: Theme made by panr

title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
body_text: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude 01 Introduction Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes 01 Introduction 02 A note about Claude’s methods 03 The Hawking-Page transition 04 The modular bootstrap 05 Conclusion Published Nov 17, 2026 Team Science Topics Discovery Agents Reasoning Beneficial Deployments See more... Related articles Science Nov 4, 2026 Investigating vault particles with Claude View more Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. The modular bootstrap As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies. To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension. Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is “written” on its surface. The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus . There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time. Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop. In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment. Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer. If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out. The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories? This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin. Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question. Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve . Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper. This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search. Conclusion These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research. Read the black hole phase transition paper here , and the modular bootstrap paper here . title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
body_text: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS | The Mozilla Blog Skip to content Mozilla Internet Culture Life Online Deep Dives Q&As Firefox Privacy & Security Firefox Features Tips and Tricks Firefox AI Mozilla VPN New Products Advertising Principles Our Work Internet Policy From the Team Download Firefox Search Search for: Internet Policy Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS November 20, 2026 Mozilla Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone. But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.  This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox. As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.     Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test. Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.  One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step. That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.   The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.  Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor. Previous Post Has Microsoft wronged you? title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
body_text: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH | Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry Home About AGITTOC 2020 2011-12 course 2014 course 2015-16 course 2017-18 course Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry November 20, 2026 Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH Posted by ravivakil under Uncategorized Leave a Comment   Updated November 22, 2026: The story so far: Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it was so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current version, in the state that it happens to be in (mid-revision). Yesterday, in the midst of meetings, I hurriedly posted it, writing: “I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is.” About 8 hours later I updated: “I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)” Links (including the draft), at which further updates can hopefully be found: John Baez and Álvaro Lozano-Robledo . This will probably be my final update on the subject, barring major new developments. For future questions about the mathematics, please contact Brian Conrad; I haven’t yet had the chance even to look at Masullo’s document, having just received it Friday (and in any case, it is out of my expertise). These are exciting times, and I look forward to the acceleration of mathematical discovery continuing! body_text: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do? 745 points by LetThingsBeDiff 3 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 853 comments I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria. In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?
