AI is the irrefutable hypothesis. reply thephyber 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Your parent is arguing what execs have been convinced of, not necessarily an obvious objective truth. AI is finding bugs that have been in PHP, Java, Ruby, NginX for years or decades. Even if "software isn't solved", AI is going to be a big part of the solution. I think the parent's comment is better read "anybody is capable of creating an app / SaaS these days, so distribution / marketing and the idea for the product are more important than implementation." This seems to be what the zeitgeist of solopreneurs are telling each other. reply zergrush 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Software written before AI is being torched and AI is fixing them now you mean. reply cbg0 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] A "fix" is generally seen as an improvement, but we're actually seeing a lot of enshittification. reply zergrush 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Code written by humans who told others they were 10x but in reality built shitty code that AI is now catching. reply gniv 2 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] > Software is solved. There are more than a hundred thousand SWEs making half a million a year writing software. The industry changed but the demand (of projects) is still outstripping supply. reply keybored 2 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] This isn’t true even at a cursory glance. We would be hearing this constantly if this was the case. People wouldn’t be “anxious” and “worried” about AI or whatever but would be talking about how to make ends meet instead of their existential feelings. So you took the opportunity of someone asking a personal and important question to spread generic FUD. Despicable. reply zergrush 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] and what is your point other than I said AI is eating software engineering jobs ? reply keybored 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] There is no point to glean for those without shame. reply zergrush 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] > And thus I paced around my office, thinking about the last five Hacker News submissions on maths, but more organically presented as if I ran into them on the street. Will computahs end dah world? Then the story circles back to whatever mundane thing I was going to do next. Ha ha: There’s nothing that I can do with humans wanting to dominate the world, sure isn’t. Pot calling kettle black here reply TZubiri 2 days ago | parent | prev [–] the question is how long do we have to wait until the guys that think like this get fired or get sued into bankruptcy. it’s an attrition game, we have to keep building small software that works, doesn’t get hacked and doesn’t go down while these accelerationists 100x into their crash. reply nharziro 2 days ago | root | parent [–] I hate to be the one to tell you this but this fantasy is not happening. The industry has changed and it's going to continue on this trajectory so you have to learn how to do this well. There are going to be companies popping up that will claim to have figured out how to build with these agents quickly, securely and in a manner that's maintainable. Those are the companies that will take our jobs. So either learn how to build like them or move on. reply F3nd0 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] > I hate to be the one to tell you this but this One would expect a phrase like that to lead into fresh factual information, not a subjective (however possibly well-informed) prediction arguing a point very similar to the one they were contesting in the first place. reply nharziro 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] This is a completely useless comment and adds nothing to the conversation. You're trying very hard to sound intelligent, but it's not working. reply TZubiri 2 days ago | root | parent | prev [–] > so you have to learn how to do this well. I get that you believe that agent development is good, but why are you trying to convince me to join? for my own good? or is it cultish even if you assume vibecoding is revolutionary, there’s still going to be an oversupply of vibecoders, and virgin programmers are going to be quite rare, in fact it’s already happening vibeocders lose capacity to go back to actually writing and reading code, and the vibecoding force is composed of non technical folk, and technical folk alike. Technical folk degrade their experience by coalescing skillsets And I just haven’t seen a big leap in software, maybe lots of vulns are discovered? Vibecoding still hasn’t brought anything major like Chatgpt, wikipedia, uber, iphone, just slop and cves reply nharziro 2 days ago | root | parent [–] I think you have your head in the sand. Good organizations are not "vibecoding" . I'm not trying convince you to join anything. It's up to you, but if you think orgs will wait for you to do everything manually because you refuse to recognize the moment you're going to be out of a job. There will be someone else who can do the same work at a fraction of the time and ultimately that's what matters. You can make llms write good and maintainable code, people are already proving this. That doesn't mean they're just throwing llms on their codebase and writing slop. I was like you once too until a model came out and was able to do something I could do that previous models couldn't. reply TZubiri 2 days ago | root | parent [–] Just a small technical side note I do believe that vibecoding and agentic engineering are different. I take the formal definition of vibecoding to be based on Karpathy's tweet about using an LLM to write code without ever seeing the code or caring about it, whether this is done by non-technical or technical folk, it's predominantly done by non-technical. What you are describing about professional programmers sounds more like agentic engineering or whatever you want to call it, but I'd say it is distinct. That said, both techniques can produce slop, and I am specializing in being the rare breed of programmers that do neither, maybe it's too an extreme position, but I derive a bigger advantage from being able to provide a no-LLM guarantee than by whatever performance improvement I might get from LLMs. Even if it's suboptimal, it's my niche. reply nharziro 2 days ago | root | parent [–] There is not going to be positions for people like you in the market. What you're doing isn't at all special. I don't know why you think this niche is worth paying for. reply TZubiri 2 days ago | root | parent [–] Because all of the employed programmers that I know have been pushed to either vibecode or do agentic engineering. In terms of supply, I think that I am now in the minority in terms of AI engineering rather than the majority. It's not special to do AI assisted engineering. In terms of demand side, it may very well be true that there's more demand for AI assisted engineers (although I would argue contrary, it's a hard debate). I'm just making the argument that supply side, I believe there's not many devs like me left, and that's what I'm doing, wish me luck Here's an example, suppose that you need someone to audit the work of an AI assisted engineer, or you need someone to verify the work of an AI assisted engineer (a work whose demand is increasing now as a majority of the workforce is AI assisted), then naturally you need someone that is different and has a different technique, an AI assisted engineer is probably going to give similar results and evaluate the work positively. A raw engineer is going to be a bit more critical, which is precisely what you look for in an audit. Similarly with redundant systems, AI assisted engineers can build great systems maybe, sure, but if you want an alternative for redundancy purposes to reduce downtime, whether internal to a company or externally through competition, you will want the second system to be as different as possible, if you use the same techniques it's not going to be very redundant, there's a case for symmetric redundancy, but there's also a lot of asymmetric redundancy, in that case too there's going to be a demand for non AI engineers. Finally consider any case where the AI needs to be trained, you can't train an AI on AI output, if there's a novel problem to solve, you can only train it on the work of non AI engineers like me. There you have it, at least 3 market demands for non AI assisted engineering, and an argument that the supply for us is more limited than the opposite. I wish you good luck in the battlefield as well. reply nharziro 2 days ago | root | parent [–] You're wrong on so many levels I don't know where to start..I don't think you realize how much these models have improved in the last year. Companies won't hire you to audit "ai assisted engineers"..the way you're speaking I'm pretty sure you're unemployed. There is no way you're working in the industry at this moment and thinking you'd find any work this way. Your goal should be building the agentic systems to the audit instead of attempting to be the audior yourself. I genuinely think you have no idea where the industry stands at the moment. You're going to get left behind . reply Guidelines | FAQ | Lists | API | Security | Legal | Apply to YC | Contact Search:

title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
body_text: We promoted developers into architects without informing them Developer forever Home Posts About Contact Read my posts Read my posts All posts We promoted developers into architects without informing them Mani Doraisamy Nov 20, 2026 7 5 Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements: First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID. All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load. What is the right code for this? If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have: Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload. In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack. Why AI won’t push back AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen. Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app. Your new job is to architect AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to: Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code. You can be the solution to this problem. You can understand the tradeoffs[1], define the architecture, design the datamodel and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement to coding tools that changes your architecture or design, they have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability. If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding. Your future as a developer In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect[2]. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you. Notes: [1] Ultimately, you have limited resources. Architecture is about trading off some requirements, so that your app can run with limited resources. Take CAP theorem as an example. You have to trade off consistency or availability or partition tolerance for your database. If you don't understand that tradeoff and ask AI to build a database that has all 3, it would reinvent Google Spanner++ and expect Google scale datacenter to run it. Or, AI will make the tradeoff for you and you end up with the same neutered architecture as every other non developer. [2] This post is trending on HN . Some have correctly pointed out that good developers already do architecture and bad architects propose ivory tower architecture that falls apart during implementation. I have built ivory tower architecture whenever I am handsoff. This will become more common with AI, if we don't debug its code or don't hand code critical parts of the app from time to time. So, don't stop coding completely, but it's not a full time job anymore. 7 Like forum 5 share Share Comments · 5 Srinivasa Prasanna Nov 20, 2026 Mani - could adopting a method like spec-driven development have helped here ? Reply Anh Le Nov 21, 2026 @斯里尼瓦萨·普拉萨纳 在这个案例中，如果你的规格不是从架构层面，而是从需求层面出发的就没有 Reply Halberdus Ravenheim Nov 21, 2026 "stop missing the coding" The coding was the fun part and I never wanted this promotion. Reply Mani Doraisamy Nov 21, 2026 @Srinivasa Prasanna Could be, but it seems requirements heavy and light on architecture/design. Reply Mani Doraisamy Nov 21, 2026 @Halberdus Ravenheim Me too (I literally named this blog "Developer forever"). But that doesnt answer the economic viablity question. Will companies pay for developers to code, if AI generates better code faster at a fraction of the cost? So, this promotion is inevitable and its better to set that expectation clearly. title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
body_text: If you can’t explain something in simple terms, you don’t understand it KOTTKE DOT ORG KOTTKE DOT ORG MENU Member Login Home Membership Newsletter Goods Search Archive + Tags About/Contact dark mode light mode Advertise here with Carbon Ads Socials & More Newsletter RSS Feed Bluesky Mastodon This site is made possible by member support . 💞 Big thanks to Arcustech for hosting the site and offering amazing tech support. When you buy through links on kottke.org, I may earn an affiliate commission. Thanks for supporting the site! kottke.org. home of fine hypertext products since 1998. Beloved by 86.47% of the web. 🍔   💀   📸   😭   🕳️   🤠   🎬   🥔 × close posted Jun 15, 2017 by Jason Kottke  ·  gift link If you can’t explain something in simple terms, you don’t understand it In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics . Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture . From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 issue of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine : Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.” John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well: Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely. Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine , rubber bands , how trains go around curves , and magnets . Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets , he says: I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with. Feynman was also quoted as saying: I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics. Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read: What I cannot create, I do not understand. title: Open Social Web Alliance
body_text: Open Social Web Alliance – OSW-Alliance.net Skip to content Open Social Web Alliance Start Policy Paper Who we are / Contact A better internet for everyone is possible. Today. How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing? The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers. Read the policy paper (PDF) The Vision A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on. The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide. A critical mass of users in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces. This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols. Read the policy paper (PDF) The Challenges The idea of an Open Social Web is not new. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active users, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill. For many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch? We have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success. Read the policy paper (PDF) The Path An ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap shows how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is big. But the levers are there. As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure). Our roadmap envisions that the German federal government will explicitly support the Alliance, for instance by acting as patron of an Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026, to which everyone with an interest in the OSW would be invited. At the summit, the Alliance would adopt its charter, setting out how it admits new members and how it intends to implement its governance going forward (see Section 2.2, Governance). By spring 2027, public funding for the infrastructure would be in place, along with a first core funding round of public and private capital for innovation and applications (see Section 2.3, Funding). The Alliance would publish its first Social Web Health Report, featuring findings from user surveys, legal, technical and academic analyses, and clear recommendations for further development (see Section 2.4, Appeal). In parallel, the federal and state governments would ensure that the legal basis for cooperation between public service media, other media, business and civil society is established (see Section 2.5, Public Mandate). The federal government would also champion the OSW idea at EU level, for instance through an implementation push for effective digital legislation. As key stakeholders such as the federal government adopt OSW applications as their primary channel of communication, influential creators and publishers would follow suit, and central political debates would quickly shift to the Open Social Web. Taken together, these measures would reduce the influence and appeal of today’s dominant Big Tech platforms. Read the policy paper (PDF) A better internet doesn’t build itself. The Open Social Web Alliance is looking for allies: people and organisations who are convinced that genuine social networks can create real value. We look forward to hearing from you. Got better ideas than ours? Even better! Get in touch Copyright 2023 – OSWA / Neve FSE theme German English

title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
body_text: Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis | What's new What's new Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao Home About Career advice On writing Books Mastodon+ Applets Subscribe to feed Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis 20 November, 2026 in math.AP , math.NT | Tags: AI , incompressible Euler equations , Levent Alpöge , Matei Coiculescu , Navier-Stokes equations , Riemann hypothesis , Tristan Buckmaster | by Terence Tao Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are: Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions , which is formalized in Lean here . Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization . Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof. Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task. See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.
